lesson.title: Working Backward: Finding the Score Behind the Percentile
lesson.summary: Inverse normal calculations start from a known probability or percentile and work backward through the normal table and the standardization formula to find the original raw value, reversing the usual process of finding a normal probability.
lesson.body:
Finding a normal probability starts with a value and ends with a percentage: given a score, what proportion of the distribution falls below it. Inverse normal calculations reverse that entire process: given a percentage or probability, what value produces it. This kind of question shows up constantly in practice, phrased as things like what score marks the 90th percentile, or what cutoff separates the top 10 percent of applicants from the rest, and it requires running the standardize-then-look-up process from finding normal probabilities backward.

The reversed process has three steps. First, identify the target cumulative probability, the area to the left of the unknown value. Second, search the body of the standard normal table for that probability, or the closest value to it, and read off the z-score attached to it, essentially looking up the table in reverse. Third, convert that z-score back into the original units using a rearranged version of the standardization formula: x equals mu plus z times sigma, rather than solving for z as before.

Suppose IQ scores are approximately normal with a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15, and the question asks for the score marking the 95th percentile, the value below which 95 percent of scores fall. Searching the standard normal table for a cumulative probability of 0.95 leads to a z-score of about 1.645, a well-known landmark value since it appears so often in practice. Converting back to the original scale: x equals 100 plus 1.645 times 15, which is 100 plus 24.675, or 124.675, typically rounded to about 124.7. So a score of roughly 124.7 marks the 95th percentile of this IQ distribution, meaning about 95 percent of people score below it and about 5 percent score above it.

The same process works just as well for a lower tail. Suppose the question instead asks for the cutoff marking the bottom 10 percent of IQ scores. A cumulative probability of 0.10 corresponds to a z-score of about negative 1.28, the negative sign reflecting that this cutoff lies below the mean. Converting back: x equals 100 plus negative 1.28 times 15, which is 100 minus 19.2, or 80.8. So a score of about 80.8 marks the bottom 10 percent of this distribution, meaning roughly 10 percent of people score below 80.8.

Inverse normal calculations complete the toolkit built across quartiles, the five-number summary, the normal distribution, standardization, and normal probabilities. Where the forward process moves from a value to a probability, this reversed process moves from a probability back to a value, and together the two directions allow any question about an approximately normal variable, whether it starts with a score or starts with a percentile, to be answered with the same underlying machinery: standardize, use the table, and convert between raw values and z-scores as the question demands.
